podcast.title: Disappearance from Embassy Hotel (February 1, 1995)
podcast.body: Richey Edwards walked out of room 516 of the Embassy Hotel on Bayswater Road in London at 7:00 am on February 1, 1995, and disappeared forever, the day he was supposed to fly to the US for a promo tour with bandmate James Dean Bradfield. Leading up to his disappearance, he had withdrawn £200 daily for two weeks, accumulating nearly £3,000 in cash. He left behind a packed suitcase, toiletries, a bottle of Prozac, and a carefully wrapped box for a 19-year-old female friend with a note that said, "I love you." His car was found abandoned at a service station two weeks later, suggesting someone had been living in it. He was officially presumed dead in November 2008, and his disappearance remains one of modern Britain's greatest missing person mysteries. "On February 1st, 1995... he walked out of the hotel at 7 in the morning and disappeared forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disappearance in February 1995
podcast.body: Just before he was due to embark on a major press tour of America in February 1995, Richey Edwards disappeared. He left his London hotel, made a final withdrawal from a bank machine, abandoned his car in the countryside, and has never been seen again, with his fate remaining unknown. "But then in February 1995, just as Richie was supposed to leave for a major press tour of America, he disappeared."

podcast.title: Admiration for Bobby Sands
podcast.body: One of Richie's childhood heroes was Bobby Sands, an IRA member who died at the age of 27 after a 65-day hunger strike in prison. This admiration provides insight into Richie's fascination with extreme forms of protest and self-sacrifice. "Interestingly, one of Richie's heroes as a kid was Bobby Sans, the IRA member who killed himself in prison by going on a hunger strike."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ambitious Rock Star with Charisma
podcast.body: From the outset, Richie aspired to be a rock star whose existence "meant something." Despite minimal musical ability, his glamorous look, prominent cheekbones, and intense charisma captivated audiences, often leading them to mistakenly assume he was the band's leader. "He had zero musical ability. Oh, sure, he had a guitar on stage, but he was mostly just miming with his amp turn down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anorexia and Self-Control
podcast.body: Richie suffered from anorexia, which appeared to be linked to a deep-seated need for self-control, possibly serving as an alternative coping mechanism to his self-harm. At 5'8", he weighed an alarming 84 pounds during his final university exams, highlighting the severity of his condition. "Alcoholism became a problem. So did anorexia, which appeared to be related to a need to exhibit self-control, perhaps as an alternative to his need to self-harm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Beloved Cocker Spaniel, Snoopy
podcast.body: Richie was devoted to his cocker spaniel, Snoopy. The dog's death at the age of 17 on January 17, 1995, left Richie inconsolable, contributing significantly to his emotional fragility in the days leading up to his disappearance. "Three days after Snoopy, his beloved cocker spaniel died at the age of 17. Richie was inconsolable, and with the band tensions and a relationship breakdown, he must have felt that the universe was crashing down around him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diagnoses of Borderline Personality Disorder and Asperger's
podcast.body: While at Priory Hospital, Richie was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder, a then-newly named condition explaining his issues with identity, relationships, and occasional dissociation. A later diagnosis of Asperger's (now a form of autism) further elucidated his laser focus and insistence on strict routines. "Two weeks into his stay at the primary, Richie was diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, a newly named condition at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Early Life and Mental Health Trigger
podcast.body: Richie experienced a happy childhood in Blackwood, South Wales, stating, "Up to the age of 13, I was ecstatically happy." However, upon moving from his nan's home and starting comprehensive school, he felt "everything started to go wrong." His self-harm behaviors reportedly began around the time of his grandmother's death. "Then I moved from my nan and started at a comprehensive school and everything started to go wrong."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intellectual and Literary Figure
podcast.body: Richie was the intellectual force behind the Manic Street Preachers, well-versed in figures like Karl Marx, Albert Camus, Sylvia Plath, Dostoevsky, JD Salinger, Jack Kerouac, and Joseph Conrad, as well as the Beat Poets. He meticulously rehearsed philosophical and literary quotes for interviews, solidifying his role as the band's literary expert. "Richie knew about Karl Marx, Albert Kamu, Sylvia Plath, Dostoevsky, JD Salinger, Jack Kerawak, Joseph Conrad, and all the beat poets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nickname "Richie Manic"
podcast.body: Richie Edwards was known by the nickname "Richie Manic," a name he preferred to be called. This moniker reflected his stage persona and identity within the band. "The band featured Richie James Edwards or Richie Manic, as he'd like to be called."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Obsession with Fictional Disappearances
podcast.body: Richie frequently discussed the 1970s TV show *The Rise and Fall of Reginald Parent*, about an executive who fakes his own death during a midlife crisis. He was also obsessed with Francis Ford Coppola's *Apocalypse Now*, particularly Marlon Brando's mysterious disappearance to a South Pacific island after the film wrapped, suggesting a fascination with vanishing without a trace. "Richie would often talk to visitors of an old 1970s TV show called The Rise and Fall of Reginald Parent. Reginald Parent was a successful executive who faked his own death during a midlife crisis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Roadie to Band Member
podcast.body: Richey Edwards initially worked as a roadie for the Manic Street Preachers before he was eventually integrated as a full-fledged member of the band. "Richie Edwards roadied for the Manic Street preachers before he ended up as a full-fledged member."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Struggles with Mental Health and Self-Harm
podcast.body: Richie openly discussed his battle with depression and frequent self-harm, which started in high school and included cutting himself and stubbing cigarettes on his arms. He found cutting to be a logical outlet for emotional pain, stating, "When I cut myself, I feel so much better. All the little things that might have been annoying me certainly seemed so trivial because I'm concentrating on the pain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Talented and Self-Destructive
podcast.body: Described as a "tremendously talented songwriter" who was concurrently "hopelessly self-destructive," which made him a compelling subject for journalists. "And they love to write about guitarist Richie Edwards, a tremendously talented songwriter who was also hopelessly self-destructive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unresolved Trust Fund for His Estate
podcast.body: If Richey Edwards is not deceased, "millions of pounds" of his earnings are being held in a trust fund somewhere, creating an unresolved financial situation. "If he's dead, well that's one thing. But what if he's not? Then there's a lot of money being kept in a trust fund somewhere, and we're talking millions of pounds."

xref.title: Post-Disappearance Regrouping and Success
xref.body: After Richey Edwards' disappearance, the band successfully "regrouped" and went on to become "one of the most successful bands they ever come out of Wales," selling millions of albums and concert tickets globally.
